about.title: About this project
about.whatIsThisContent:
KH Tools is a volunteer-maintained, open-source directory that gathers independent apps created by fellow Jehovah's Witnesses to support various congregation activities — things like audio and video management, field service tracking, territory organization, and more.

Over the years, many brothers have developed helpful tools on their own initiative. The challenge is that these apps are scattered across the internet, and it can be hard to know which ones exist or how they compare. This project brings them together in one place with practical information to help you make an informed choice.
about.whyContent:
There is no single place where you can find and compare all the independent apps built for congregation use. If you've ever searched for "an app to manage meeting media" or "a territory management tool," you've probably found fragmented information across forums, social media, and word of mouth.

This directory solves that by organizing everything in one spot, with clear comparisons, feature breakdowns, and privacy notes for each app.
about.howItWorksContent:
Each category (e.g. Audio & Video, Field Service) lists all the independent apps we've found and reviewed. For each app, we provide:

• A brief description of what it does
• Which platforms it supports
• A feature comparison table
• Privacy and trust information
• Pros and cons
• A suggested pick ("Verdict")

The verdict is our honest read based on the available information — but every congregation is different, and the final call is always yours.
about.submitContent: If you know of an app that isn't listed here, please open an issue on GitHub. Simply provide the app name and a link — we'll take care of researching and reviewing it.
about.disclaimerContent: This project is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or connected to the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Pennsylvania or any of its related entities. All apps listed here are independently developed by publishers who are Jehovah’s Witnesses. Any decision to use or rely on these apps is entirely at the user’s discretion.

audio-video.summary: Practical recommendation: Solin has the edge for direct meeting use because it combines a more fluid live workflow, an app that remains responsive during projection, prepared pan/zoom, an integrated tabbed browser, native Zoom integration, attendance counting, a gentler learning curve, and stronger practical privacy. Meeting Media Manager remains a strong solution, especially because it is open source, supports Linux, has broad documentation, automatic background music, and a longer public history; Solin is also still a recent project, with its first public changelog entry on March 19, 2026. Even so, in this specific audio/video practical-use comparison, Solin appears to be the stronger choice.

meeting-scheduling.summary: Context-dependent tie: Hourglass is the more accessible option for a congregation that wants to get started quickly, with browser-based use, mobile apps, notifications, and donation-based cost. NW Scheduler is the more cautious choice when the priority is keeping the administrative core desktop/local, with less cloud dependency and documented end-to-end encrypted sharing. Since both cover scheduling and assignments well, the decision mainly depends on how much weight you give to collaborative convenience versus local data control.

solin.description: Free desktop application for meeting visual support, with automatic weekly media downloads, second-screen projection, integrated browser, playlists, local Wi-Fi transfer, and Zoom/OBS integrations.
details: The home page presents Solin as an app for songs, videos, images, and projector output, showing version 1.11.0.0 on May 7, 2026.
The app automatically downloads songs and videos for the current and next week, and the features page says it works offline once media has been downloaded.
The projector receives videos, images, PDFs, JWPub files, and other media in a clean fullscreen view while controls remain on the main monitor.

The integrated browser lets the operator navigate inside Solin, project images/videos, or stream a tab live; the changelog records live tab streaming improvements, 16:9 lock, and a new browser engine with modern video support.
In practical use reviewed here, Solin lets the operator keep using the app during projection, prepare pan/zoom on the main screen, and only then send or reset the projector output.
Wi-Fi transfer uses a QR code and the local network, with no account, cloud, or cable; the privacy policy says files shared this way stay between devices on the same network.

Recent changelog entries added native macOS support, multiple profiles, playlist sections/colors, linked folders, Zoom Meetings integration, OBS integration, overlay toolbar, and Memorial calculation/media.

The About page says the main installers target Windows 10+ and macOS 13+, but there is a legacy installer for Windows 8/8.1; that version is described as an adaptation of the current app, may be slower or unstable, and will not receive support for newer Solin versions.
The privacy policy says the app collects no personal data, usage statistics, error reports, or telemetry; it makes GET calls for version checks with an anonymous UUID and for global notifications.
In the practical test reviewed here, that stated behavior matched the observed traffic: no Solin telemetry, analytics, or error-reporting requests were identified.
The site says no account or subscription is required; the terms say Solin is free, has no paid features, is provided as-is, and is not affiliated with or endorsed by any official organization.
The About page says Solin is free and that this will not change; no donation page was identified on the official site during this review.
In a Windows installation observed during this review, the installed app occupied about 176 MB; this number is contextual and may vary by version, platform, and local cache.
The app is not open source and the terms prohibit reverse engineering.
pros: Very flexible projection workflow: the operator can keep navigating the app while something is projected.
Direct pan/zoom that can be prepared before sending to the projector.
Integrated tabbed browser with live projection of a specific tab.
Native Zoom integration, including meeting features and attendance counting documented in the changelog.
Explicit privacy policy that matches the observed practical traffic: no personal data, telemetry, or error reports.
Gentler learning curve for operators who need to adopt the app quickly.
Observed installation is considerably smaller than M3 on the Windows system reviewed.
Local QR/Wi-Fi transfer without an account or cloud.
cons: Closed source, with terms that prohibit reverse engineering.
No Linux version listed on the official site as of this review.
Newer project with a shorter public history than M3.
No documented automatic background music feature equivalent to M3.

meeting-media-manager.description: Open-source cross-platform app for downloading, organizing, and presenting meeting media, with Zoom/OBS support, background music, watched folders, JWPUB/JWLPLAYLIST, multiple profiles, and extensive documentation.
details: The documentation describes M3 as a comprehensive app for Windows, macOS, and Linux that downloads, organizes, and presents pictures and videos for meetings in any language available on the official website.

The repository is public, licensed AGPL-3.0-or-later, and the README lists automatic downloads, presentation tools, Zoom, OBS, multiple congregations, playlists, JWPUB, Bible audio, public talks, and external media import.
The FAQ lists support for Windows 10+, macOS 10.15+, and Linux AppImage, with minimum requirements of 4 GB RAM and 6 GB free disk space, recommending 8 GB and 15 GB for cache.
The documentation says meeting data is stored locally on the computer, media is downloaded directly from the official website, and the code is available for review.
The app uses Sentry in the Electron process to capture exceptions and crashes; the FAQ describes this as limited collection for bug reporting.

The code also initializes Sentry in the renderer with session integration and browser/router tracing, using tracesSampleRate 1; this enables performance, navigation, and interaction events beyond errors.

In real traffic analyzed on May 8, 2026, the payload sent to Sentry included in-app navigation transactions, timestamps and transaction durations, HTTP request spans, store/console breadcrumbs, a local file:// URL with a path that can reveal the Windows username, User-Agent, locale/timezone, and hardware signals such as device memory and CPU core count.
Presentation includes media controls, shortcuts, custom timing, pan/zoom for images and videos, an external media window, monitor detection, and website presentation for trusted sites.

In practical use reviewed here, M3 concentrates control in the presentation flow; pan/zoom is performed through thumbnails/controls, without the same direct preview and separate send/reset workflow as Solin.
The website feature opens a separate window for trusted sites; the code limits JW domains to jw.org, jwevent.org, and stream.jw.org, with trusted CDNs for content.

The recent changelog shows very active maintenance: JW Stream added to mirrorable sites, meeting timer, Memorial media out of beta, automatic meeting schedule sync, security hardening, media fixes, watch folders, and frequent dependency updates.
The FAQ says donations are not accepted and never will be, in harmony with the idea of providing freely.
In a Windows installation observed during this review, the installed app occupied about 568 MB; this number is contextual and may vary by version, platform, and local cache.
pros: AGPL open source, allowing real auditability of the app's behavior.
Supports Windows, macOS, and Linux.
Longer, mature history with an active repository, broad documentation, and community.
Automatic background music is well documented, with stopping before the meeting and one-click restart.
Documentation covers requirements, limitations, setup, FAQ, contribution, and troubleshooting.
Auto-export and watched-folder workflows are well documented for backup and home-to-Kingdom Hall work.
cons: Practical Sentry telemetry is broader than the limited bug-reporting description suggests.
During projection, the workflow is less free for navigating to other areas of the app.
Because it brings together many modules and options, initial setup may require more care for less experienced operators.
Practical pan/zoom depends on thumbnails/controls, not direct visual pre-adjustment on the projected media.
Website presentation is more restricted and opens in a separate window, not as an in-app tabbed browser.

nw-scheduler.description: Desktop software for Windows and macOS, with the NW Publisher companion app for publishers. It covers Life and Ministry, public talks, field service, carts, duties, territories, secretary workflows, and other congregation workflows.
details: The administrative core is installed locally on Windows or macOS; the NW Publisher app for iOS, Android, and Amazon is complementary and depends on the congregation using NW Scheduler.
The Life and Ministry meeting scheduler includes main and auxiliary classes, Auto-Assign, recommended students, and detailed part history.

Its scope goes beyond meetings: secretary records, publisher records, monthly reports, public talks, service groups, carts, territories, cleaning, duties, maintenance, circuit overseer visits, information board, literature, and tasks.
Congregation Sharing is optional, disabled by default, and uses OAuth 2.0, TLS 1.2, and end-to-end encryption with AES-256; according to the vendor documentation, keys stay on the local device.
The documentation says that, by default, data stays only on the local computer and that developers, administrators, and support personnel cannot view or edit congregation data.
The registration page lists a 60-day free trial and annual licenses, including Individual at US$12, Congregation Silver at US$29, and Congregation Gold at US$39 as of this review.
The vendor states that the program is not official or endorsed by the organization, and that each congregation should make its own choice.
pros: Desktop/local model favors direct data control by the congregation.
Very broad set of modules in one program.
Strong scheduling features: Auto-Assign, part history, and multiple congregation areas.
Extensive documentation about encryption, sharing, and data retention.
NW Publisher extends access to publishers on iOS and Android.
cons: It is not a web solution: the main administrative work depends on desktop installation.
Paid annual license after the trial period.
Heavier workflow for congregations that want immediate browser-based collaboration.
The source code is not open.

hourglass.description: Web application for congregations with mobile apps for publishers. It organizes publishers, groups, contacts, attendance, territories, schedules, assignments, reports, and notifications.
details: Administrative use happens through the web service app.hourglass-app.com, with apps for iOS and Android; first-time mobile app use requires an invitation from the congregation.

The official page lists organization of publishers, groups, emergency contacts, meeting attendance, and territories, plus schedules for cleaning, field service, public witnessing, midweek and weekend meetings, audio/video, attendants, and language groups.
Assignments can notify assignees immediately, with the option to accept or decline, and publishers can submit field service reports from their phones.
Hourglass says it can import data from KHS, NW Scheduler, or TSWIN and export congregation data as PDF, DOCX, CSV, or JSON.
Documented security includes encryption in transit and at rest, redundant hosting dedicated to Hourglass, and optional end-to-end encryption for personal data.
The privacy policy states that Hourglass uses AWS, collects email for registered users, stores data entered by congregation representatives, and does not process payments inside Hourglass itself.
The FAQ says to consult direction provided by the local branch office to ensure Hourglass use is compliant with applicable guidance.

The separate SMPW module covers zones, locations, publishers, manual/automatic/open scheduling, Auto-Fill, and communications by email, SMS, WhatsApp, and Signal; this was not counted here as general Auto-Assign for meeting parts.
The FAQ states that no payment is required and that the service is supported by voluntary donations.
pros: Works in the browser and reduces dependency on desktop installation.
No required payment, supported by donations.
Official mobile apps in app stores, with congregation invitation and notifications.
Good coverage of schedules, reports, territories, and assignments in one centralized interface.
Imports from NW Scheduler, KHS, and TSWIN and exports to useful formats.
cons: The web/cloud model requires careful evaluation of local data-protection direction.
End-to-end encryption is described as optional, not mandatory for all data by default.
Depends on the online service for primary use.
The source code is not open.
